summary.text: A recurrence for the continued fraction, together with a congruence for its numerator modulo \(5n-4\), gives \(a(n)=(5n-4)/\gcd(5n-4,\prod_{j=3}^n j)\). For existence, choose \(c\in\{1,2,3,4\}\) so that \(n=(cp+4)/5\) is integral (handling \(p=11\) at \(n=3\)); conversely, \(a(n)=p\) forces \(5n-4=cp\) with \(1\le c<5\) and \(n<p\), since otherwise the product contains enough factors to make the reduced denominator \(1\), and reduction modulo \(5\) then fixes \(c\) and hence \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
C_n=\frac1{\displaystyle 2-\frac3{\displaystyle 3-\frac4{\displaystyle 4-\frac5{\ddots-\frac{n-1}{\displaystyle (n-1)-\frac n{n+4}}}}}}
\]
for \(n\ge 3\), and let \(a(n)\) be the denominator of \(C_n\) after reduction to lowest terms. We prove that every odd prime \(p\ne3,5\) occurs as exactly one value \(a(n)\), \(n\ge3\).

We first derive a formula for \(a(n)\).

For a fixed \(n\ge4\), define integers \(P_k=P_k(n)\), for \(3\le k\le n\), backwards by
\[
P_n=n+4,
\qquad
P_{n-1}=n^2+2n-4,
\]
and, for \(3\le k<n-1\),
\[
P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}. \tag{1}
\]
These are the numerator continuants of the successive tails. Indeed, the last tail is
\[
(n-1)-\frac n{n+4}
 =\frac{(n-1)(n+4)-n}{n+4}
 =\frac{n^2+2n-4}{n+4}
 =\frac{P_{n-1}}{P_n}.
\]
If the tail beginning with \(k+1\) is \(P_{k+1}/P_{k+2}\), then the tail beginning with \(k\) is
\[
k-\frac{k+1}{P_{k+1}/P_{k+2}}
 =\frac{kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}}{P_{k+1}}
 =\frac{P_k}{P_{k+1}},
\]
which gives (1).

To see at the same time that none of the divisions used here is by zero, consider
\[
L_k=(k-1)P_k-k(k-2)P_{k+1}.
\]
Using (1), a direct expansion gives
\[
L_k=L_{k+1}\qquad(3\le k<n-1).
\]
At the boundary,
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{n-1}
&=(n-2)(n^2+2n-4)-(n-1)(n-3)(n+4)\\
&=5n-4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently
\[
(k-1)P_k-k(k-2)P_{k+1}=5n-4 \tag{2}
\]
for every \(3\le k\le n-1\). Starting from \(P_n=n+4>0\) and proceeding backwards in (2), we find that every \(P_k\) is positive: if \(P_{k+1}>0\), then
\[
(k-1)P_k=(5n-4)+k(k-2)P_{k+1}>0.
\]
Thus the tail calculations above are legitimate.

Taking \(k=3\) in (2) gives
\[
2P_3-3P_4=5n-4. \tag{3}
\]
Since the tail beginning at \(3\) is \(P_3/P_4\), (3) shows that
\[
C_n
=\frac1{2-3/(P_3/P_4)}
=\frac{P_3}{2P_3-3P_4}
=\frac{P_3}{5n-4}. \tag{4}
\]
It follows that
\[
a(n)=\frac{5n-4}{\gcd(5n-4,P_3)}. \tag{5}
\]

We next replace the second entry of this gcd by a simple product. Put
\[
B_n=\prod_{j=3}^{n}j=3\cdot4\cdots n,
\qquad q_n=5n-4.
\]
We claim that, more generally,
\[
P_k\equiv \bigl(5(n-k)+6\bigr)\prod_{j=k}^{n}j\pmod{q_n} \tag{6}
\]
for \(3\le k\le n\).

This is a backward induction. For \(k=n\), the right side is \(6n\), and
\[
6n-P_n=6n-(n+4)=5n-4=q_n.
\]
For \(k=n-1\), substituting \(P_{n-1}=n^2+2n-4\) into (6) reduces, by expansion, to divisibility by \(5n-4\); explicitly,
\[
(5(n-(n-1))+6)(n-1)n-P_{n-1}
=11n(n-1)-(n^2+2n-4)
=(5n-4)(2n-1).
\]
For the induction step, insert the two congruences for \(P_{k+1}\) and \(P_{k+2}\) into
\(P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)P_{k+2}\). Using
\[
\prod_{j=k}^{n}j=k\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}j,
\qquad
\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}j=(k+1)\prod_{j=k+2}^{n}j,
\]
and collecting terms gives the right side of (6), with the remaining difference a multiple of \(5n-4\). This proves (6).

At \(k=3\), (6) says
\[
P_3\equiv (5n-9)B_n\pmod{5n-4}. \tag{7}
\]
Now
\[
\gcd(5n-4,5n-9)=1. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, their difference is \(5\), while \(5n-9\equiv1\pmod5\), so a common divisor must divide both \(5\) and a number congruent to \(1\) modulo \(5\).

Equations (7) and (8) imply
\[
\gcd(5n-4,P_3)=\gcd(5n-4,B_n). \tag{9}
\]
For completeness, if \(D\mid 5n-4\), congruence (7) gives
\[
D\mid P_3\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D\mid(5n-9)B_n.
\]
Since every divisor \(D\) of \(5n-4\) is coprime to \(5n-9\), the last condition is equivalent to \(D\mid B_n\). Thus the common divisors on the two sides of (9) are exactly the same.

Combining (5) and (9), we obtain the central formula
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
 a(n)=\frac{5n-4}{\gcd(5n-4,B_n)}}
 \qquad(n\ge4). \tag{10}
\]
At the remaining initial index,
\[
C_3=\frac1{2-3/(3+4)}=\frac7{11},
\qquad	ext{so}\qquad a(3)=11. \tag{11}
\]

We now prove existence. We will use the following immediate consequence of (10). Suppose that \(p\) is prime and that, for some positive integer \(c\),
\[
5n-4=cp,\qquad n<p,\qquad c\mid B_n. \tag{12}
\]
Because every factor of \(B_n\) lies strictly below \(p\), the prime \(p\) does not divide \(B_n\). Hence
\[
\gcd(cp,B_n)=c.
\]
More explicitly, \(c\) is a common divisor by (12), and no additional factor \(p\) can occur in the gcd; Euclid's lemma then gives the equality. Formula (10) consequently yields \(a(n)=p\).

Let \(p\) be an odd prime different from \(3\) and \(5\). Such a prime satisfies \(p\ge7\). First, if \(p=11\), equation (11) gives the occurrence \(a(3)=11\).

Assume henceforth that \(p\ne11\). Since \(p\ne5\), its residue modulo \(5\) is one of \(1,2,3,4\). Choose \(c\) and \(n\) according to the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
p\pmod5&c&n\\ \hline
1&1&(p+4)/5\\
2&3&(3p+4)/5\\
3&2&(2p+4)/5\\
4&4&(4p+4)/5.
\end{array} \tag{13}
\]
The indicated numerator is divisible by \(5\) in each row, and in every case
\[
5n-4=cp. \tag{14}
\]
Also \(n<p\): for \(c=2,3,4\), this follows from \(cp+4<5p\), since \(p>4\), and for \(c=1\) it is immediate. Each of these indices is at least \(4\). The only point requiring comment is the first row: writing \(p=5k+1\), oddness of \(p\) makes \(k\) even; if \(n=k+1<4\), then the only possible prime here is \(p=11\), which was separated already. In the other rows \(p\ge7\) directly gives \(n\ge4\).

Finally, \(c\mid B_n\). This is clear for \(c=1\); and for \(c=2,3,4\), it follows because \(B_n=3\cdot4\cdots n\) with \(n\ge4\) contains respectively a factor divisible by \(2\), the factor \(3\), and the factor \(4\). Thus (12) applies in every row of (13), proving that every eligible prime occurs.

It remains to prove uniqueness. We first establish a strong restriction on any occurrence. Let \(p\) be an odd prime with \(p\ne3,5\), and suppose
\[
n\ge3,
\qquad a(n)=p. \tag{15}
\]
We claim that there is an integer \(c\) such that
\[
1\le c<5,
\qquad 5n-4=cp. \tag{16}
\]
For \(n=3\), (11) forces \(p=11\), and (16) holds with \(c=1\). We may therefore assume \(n\ge4\).

Set
\[
G=\gcd(5n-4,B_n).
\]
By (10) and (15),
\[
5n-4=pG. \tag{17}
\]
Certainly \(G>0\). We next prove the crucial bound
\[
n<p. \tag{18}
\]
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(p\le n\). Since every eligible \(p\) is at least \(7\), equation (17) gives
\[
pG=5n-4<7n\le pn,
\]
so \(G<n\). Also \(G\ge3\). For if \(G\le2\), then, using \(p\le n\),
\[
5n-4=pG\le2p\le2n,
\]
which is impossible for \(n\ge4\).
Thus both \(p\) and \(G\) lie in the interval \([3,n]\).

If \(G\ne p\), they occur as two distinct factors in the product \(B_n=3\cdot4\cdots n\). Removing those two factors from the product shows that
\[
pG\mid B_n.
\]
By (17), this says \(5n-4\mid B_n\), and hence
\(\gcd(5n-4,B_n)=5n-4\). Formula (10) would then give \(a(n)=1\), contradicting \(a(n)=p>1\).

It remains to handle the exceptional possibility \(G=p\). In that case (17) is
\[
5n-4=p^2. \tag{19}
\]
The smallest eligible prime is \(7\). If \(p=7\), (19) would give \(5n=53\), impossible. Hence in this case \(p\ge11\). From (19),
\[
n=\frac{p^2+4}{5}\ge2p,
\]
because \(p^2+4-10p>0\) for \(p\ge11\). Therefore both \(p\) and \(2p\) are distinct members of \([3,n]\). Their product \(2p^2\) divides \(B_n\), so in particular \(p^2=5n-4\) divides \(B_n\). Once again (10) gives \(a(n)=1\), a contradiction. This proves (18).

Finally, (17), (18), and \(5n-4<5n<5p\) imply
\[
G<5.
\]
Thus (16) holds with \(c=G\).

Now suppose that the same eligible prime occurs at two indices \(n,y\ge3\):
\[
a(n)=a(y)=p.
\]
By (16), there are \(c,d\in\{1,2,3,4\}\) such that
\[
5n-4=cp,
\qquad
5y-4=dp. \tag{20}
\]
Reducing modulo \(5\) gives
\[
cp\equiv dp\equiv1\pmod5. \tag{21}
\]
Because \(p\ne5\), multiplication by \(p\) is invertible modulo \(5\), so (21) implies \(c\equiv d\pmod5\). Since both lie in \(\{1,2,3,4\}\), we have \(c=d\). Equations (20) then give \(5n-4=5y-4\), hence \(n=y\).

We have proved both existence and uniqueness: every odd prime other than \(3\) and \(5\) occurs exactly once among the reduced denominators \(a(n)\), for \(n\ge3\).
